feedback.message: Not yet. `IncV` has a value receiver, so it increments a copy and the change is lost.

hints: A value receiver works on a copy.
A pointer receiver works on the original.
exercises.solution: `IncV` increments a copy of `x`, which is discarded. Each `IncP` increments `x` itself. So `x.n` is **2**.

hints: When the outer struct has a field or method with the same name, the outer one wins.
The embedded value is still reachable by its type name.
exercises.solution: `d.Name` is the outer field, `d`; `d.Base.Name` is the embedded one, `b`. `d.Hello()` finds `Derived`'s own method first, `derived`; `d.Base.Hello()` calls `Base`'s, `base`. Output: `d b derived base`.

exercises.prompt: `countingWriter` has `func (c *countingWriter) Write(p []byte) (int, error)`. Which assignment compiles?

options.label: `var w io.Writer = &countingWriter{}`
options.feedback: Yes. The pointer type `*countingWriter` has the `Write` method, so it satisfies `io.Writer`.

options.label: `var w io.Writer = countingWriter{}`
options.feedback: Not yet. The compiler reports that countingWriter does not implement io.Writer because `Write` has a pointer receiver.

options.label: Both
options.feedback: Not yet. Methods with pointer receivers belong only to the pointer type's method set.

options.label: Neither: you must declare `implements io.Writer`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Go has no implements declaration; having the methods is enough.

hints: Which method set contains methods declared with pointer receivers?
exercises.solution: The method set of `*countingWriter` includes `Write`; the method set of `countingWriter` (the value type) does not, because calling a pointer method needs an address. So only `&countingWriter{}` can be stored in an `io.Writer`.

exercises.prompt: Why does `checkWrong("Ife") == nil` evaluate to `false` in the lesson's program, even though no error occurred?

options.label: The returned `error` interface holds a type (`*ValidationError`) with a nil value, and an interface is nil only if both type and value are nil.
options.feedback: Yes. Return the literal `nil` instead of a typed nil pointer.

options.label: Comparing an error with `nil` is not allowed; use `errors.Is`.
options.feedback: Not yet. `err != nil` is the standard check; the problem is what the function returned.

options.label: `ValidationError` has a bug in its `Error` method.
options.feedback: Not yet. `Error` is never called here; the comparison happens on the interface value itself.

options.label: Pointers can never be nil in Go.
options.feedback: Not yet. Pointers can be nil; the issue is the interface wrapped around one.

hints: An interface value is a (type, value) pair.
exercises.solution: Converting a nil `*ValidationError` to `error` produces the pair (type `*ValidationError`, value nil), which is not equal to the nil interface (no type, no value). Functions returning `error` should return the untyped `nil` when there is no error.

exercises.prompt: Which of these struct types can be compared with `==`? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `struct{ Name string; Tags []string }`
options.feedback: Not yet. Slices aren't comparable, so neither is a struct containing one; the compiler rejects `==`.

options.label: `struct{ When time.Time; Where [2]float64 }`
options.feedback: Yes. Arrays of comparable elements and structs of comparable fields are comparable (though `time.Time` values are better compared with their `Equal` method).

hints: Slices, maps and functions are the non-comparable types.
exercises.solution: A struct is comparable if all its fields are. (a) and (c) qualify; (b) contains a slice and (d) a map, so `==` on them is a compile error. Comparable structs can also be used as map keys.

exercises.prompt: You are writing `func SaveReport(dst ???, r Report) error`. Which parameter type follows Go's usual advice?

options.label: `io.Writer`
options.feedback: Yes. Asking only for what you need lets callers pass a file, a buffer, a network connection or a test double.

options.label: `*os.File`
options.feedback: Not yet. That works only with real files, which makes the function harder to test and reuse.

options.label: `any`
options.feedback: Not yet. Too broad: the function would need a type assertion to write anything, and mistakes would appear at run time.

options.label: A new 12-method `ReportStorage` interface
options.feedback: Not yet. Large interfaces are hard to satisfy; the function only needs to write bytes.

hints: What is the smallest behaviour `SaveReport` needs from its destination?
exercises.solution: "Accept interfaces, return structs." `SaveReport` only needs to write bytes, so `io.Writer` is the right parameter type: files, buffers, HTTP responses and test fakes all satisfy it.
